title: CPR, child
summary: Child from about 1 year old until puberty who is unresponsive and not breathing normally: compressions and breaths, and an AED.

steps.text: Check the scene is safe. Tap and shout. Look at the chest: is the child breathing normally?
steps.detail:
Child CPR is for children from about 1 year old until puberty (breast development in girls, underarm hair in boys). After puberty use CPR, adult. Under about 1 year use CPR, infant.

Gasping is not normal breathing. If the child is unresponsive and not breathing normally, with no signs of life, start CPR. A lay rescuer does not check for a pulse.

In children the heart usually stops because of a breathing problem (choking, drowning, illness) rather than a heart problem. That is why breaths matter so much in child CPR.

ask.q: Unresponsive and not breathing normally (or only gasping)?

steps.text: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. Send someone for an AED.
steps.detail:
If you have a phone with signal, call on speaker and start CPR at the same time. If others are present, send one for help and one for an AED.

If you are alone with no signal (AHA 2025 pediatric single-rescuer algorithm):
- If you saw the child suddenly collapse and an AED can be fetched quickly, go for help and the AED first, then start CPR.
- If you did not see the collapse, give CPR first. After about 2 minutes (about 5 rounds of 30 compressions and 2 breaths), if you are still alone, go for help and get an AED.
Off-grid, going for help may mean leaving for a long time. Shout for help as you work, and decide whether leaving is worth it.

steps.text: Lay the child on their back on a firm, flat surface. Kneel beside them.
steps.detail: A firm surface such as the floor or ground is best. If you find the child face down, roll them onto their back. Bare the chest if it is quick to do.

steps.text: Push hard and fast on the lower half of the breastbone: about 2 inches deep (one third of the chest), 100 to 120 a minute.
steps.detail:
Hand position: heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone in the centre of the chest, avoiding the very bottom tip of the breastbone. For a larger child put your other hand on top with the fingers interlaced and off the chest. For a small child one hand is enough. Either one or two hands is acceptable; use whatever gets you to the right depth.

Depth: at least one third of the depth of the chest, about 2 inches (5 cm).

Rate: 100 to 120 a minute. The CPR coach clicks the beat.

Let the chest come all the way back up after each push. Keep pauses under 10 seconds.

Keep your shoulders over your hands and your arms straight.

steps.text: After every 30 pushes, give 2 breaths. Tilt the head, lift the chin, and blow for about 1 second until the chest rises.
steps.detail:
Breaths improve survival in children, so give them if you are able and willing. If you truly cannot or will not give breaths, compression-only CPR is still far better than nothing.

Open the airway: tilt the head back slightly past the neutral position and lift the chin. If you suspect a neck injury, a jaw thrust can be used if you have been taught it; if that does not open the airway, use the head tilt and chin lift anyway.

Pinch the nose, seal your mouth over the child's mouth, and blow for about 1 second, just enough to make the chest rise. Let the air out before the second breath. Avoid big, forceful breaths.

If the first breath does not make the chest rise, re-tilt the head and check your seal before the second breath. If the second breath still does not go in, something may be blocking the airway: go straight back to compressions, and each time you open the airway look in the mouth and remove any object you can see. Never do blind finger sweeps.

Two rescuers: the ratio changes to 15 compressions to 2 breaths. The coach uses the single-rescuer ratio of 30:2.

Drowning: give CPR with breaths. A trained rescuer may start with breaths before compressions.

steps.text: When the AED arrives, turn it on and follow its prompts. Use child pads if it has them.
steps.detail:
For children under 8, use child (pediatric) pads or the AED's child setting if it has one. If there are no child pads, use the adult pads; an AED without a child setting may still be used.

Use the largest pads that fit on the chest without touching each other. If they would touch, put one in the middle of the chest and the other on the back between the shoulder blades.

Make sure nobody touches the child when the AED analyses or shocks. After a shock, or if no shock is advised, start compressions again immediately.

After drowning, start CPR with breaths before putting the AED on.

steps.text: Keep going. Swap the person doing compressions about every 2 minutes if anyone can help.
If the child starts breathing normally, roll them onto their side (recovery position) and keep watching their breathing.
steps.detail: Use the Recovery position protocol and stay with the child. If breathing becomes abnormal or stops, roll them onto their back and restart CPR.

steps.text: Responsive, or breathing normally: do not start CPR. Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.
steps.detail:
If the child is unresponsive but breathing normally and there is no reason to suspect a neck, back, hip or pelvis injury, use the Recovery position protocol.

If the child is breathing but very poorly (very slow, struggling), a trained rescuer gives breaths at about 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds.

If the child is awake but struggling to breathe, use the Choking, adult and child protocol (if something is stuck) or the Anaphylaxis protocol (severe allergic reaction).

Watch the breathing continuously. If it stops or becomes only gasping, come back to this protocol and start CPR.

donts: Do not skip breaths if you are able to give them; most child arrests start with a breathing problem.
Do not do blind finger sweeps in the mouth; remove only an object you can see.
Do not give big, forceful breaths; just enough to make the chest rise.
Do not touch the child while the AED analyses or shocks.
evacuate: Any child who needed CPR must get to hospital urgently, even if they recover.
